title: The Son, Sun of Righteousness and Giver of Every Good
english: … Lord” (Acts 10:36). On what ground, then, or how, or when could he be brought in as unlike the Father, when he has been honoured with so many oracles, so clear, so alike in manner, and in no way different from those spoken of the Father?

That the Son makes every good thing dawn, and is “the sun of righteousness and healing,” “the treasure of wisdom and knowledge,” and “light”; and that those who believe and “are not made to stumble in him” “become sons of light.”

Those, at any rate, who have sung his praises show us his Godhead in various ways, and that he presides in full over his own works. They teach that he is the giver of every good: a light good in form and doing good, a sun seen by the mind. With the unceasing light that comes from himself he makes bright the eyes of souls that do not wander and are ready to receive him. He leads them within the vantage point of contemplation and makes them see what, because of sin, they could not see before by their own nature; or he even makes the whole perfected man full of light, as the sun makes sunlike the bodies it comes upon. They teach, further, that he is also healing, and an inexhaustible and all-sufficient “treasure of wisdom and knowledge.”

And those who are sincerely disposed toward him, as toward his Father, become sons of light, since they are sons of God the Father. So Malachi proclaims: “For you who fear my name the sun of righteousness will rise, and healing in his wings” (Malachi 4:2). And Peter in his second letter: “Until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” (2 Peter 1:19). He meant, I think, the illumination that is to rise on souls at his second appearing and to make bright all that darkness holds fast. And elsewhere: “And the glory of the Lord has risen upon you” (Isaiah 60:1).

Zechariah prophesied: “If anything is good, it is his; and if anything is beautiful, it will come from him” (Zechariah 9:17). And Paul said of him to the Colossians: “In whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden” (Colossians 2:3); and to the Romans: “For the Scripture says,” he writes, “‘Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.’ For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord of all is rich toward all who call on him. For everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:11-13).
But what name of the Son do they call on, who call him, the glorious victor, the Saviour of heaven and earth and sea, neither uncreated God nor Son of one substance with the Father?

John likewise says of him: “While you have the light, believe in the light, so that you may become sons of light” (John 12:36). For after death, he says, there is no repentance, as David too sings: “But in Hades who will confess to you?” (Psalm 6:5). And again, from the Saviour: “Go and tell John what you see and hear: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the dead are raised, and the poor have the good news preached to them; and blessed is whoever is not made to stumble in me” (Matthew 11:4-6).

For what will he say about those who are led astray and those who lead them astray? Isaiah foretold it: “My people, those who call you blessed lead you astray and confuse the path of your feet. But now the Lord will take his stand for judgment and will set his people for judgment. The Lord himself will come to judgment with the elders of the people and with their rulers. But you, why did you set my vineyard on fire?” (Isaiah 3:12-14).

The Lord himself will come to judgment with the teachers and rulers, not as one who is himself to be judged by another, but to convict them, as he declares in another place: “Come, and let us go to judgment, says the Lord” (Isaiah 1:18): “what things,” he says, “came to you from me, and what things have been done by you to me and to my servants.”

For he calls the world, or the people, a “vineyard.” The interpreters of the heretics and of the Jews made it liable to the fire of Gehenna by their blasphemous teaching; and the rulers, who did not make its welfare their own concern but abused their authority, wronged it in many and various ways.

added_allusions.reason: “what things came to you from me, and what things have been done by you to me” echoes the Lord’s lawsuit with his people (“My people, what have I done to you?”); Didymus gives it as the Lord’s words but it matches no verse exactly

translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

2026-11-11 (claude-sumfix2-e-u09): retranslated from the Greek. The old draft printed edition numbers (28.n, 28.1-28.7) and a page number ('28.6 33') inside the sentences, merged the chapter title into the first paragraph, garbled 27.66 ('how could you be inserted'), 28.4 ('the one from his second appearance is about to rise to the souls as a light'), 28.7 ('for he says, he says'; 'believing upon it'), 28.8 (καλλίνικον as 'the fine net'; the sense of the question reversed) and 28.14 ('guilty ... regarding the fire'). Abbreviated references written in full; Romans 10:11 and 10:12-13 joined as 10:11-13; Isaiah 43:26 corrected to Isaiah 1:18; Acts 10:36, Zechariah 9:17 and the full Isaiah 3:12-14 checked.
